variants.name: Hand-rolled cooperative token (or concurrent-ruby Cancellation)
variants.idiom_name: shared cancellation object with canceled?/check! polled at safe points
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby ships no cancellation object, so the token is built from the synchronization primitives: a shared object whose cancel! flips a flag and broadcasts a ConditionVariable (or pushes a sentinel), and whose canceled?/check! the worker calls each cycle. concurrent-ruby packages exactly this as Concurrent::Cancellation - explicitly documented as cooperative, inspired by the .NET model, with canceled?, check!, origin.resolve and join for combining - but it lives in the edge gem and may change. The classic manual structure is therefore still the honest default here, and the token must be passed explicitly because fibers, threads and Ractors cannot see each other's thread-local state.
variants.code_sketch:
Cancellation = Struct.new(:cancelled) do        # cooperative token, shared
  def cancel! = (self.cancelled = true)
  def canceled? = cancelled
end

token = Cancellation.new(false)
Thread.new do
  until token.canceled?               # safe point
    process(queue.pop(true)) rescue sleep(0.01)
  end
end
token.cancel!                          # request; the thread stops when it checks
pitfalls: Without a ConditionVariable/Queue wakeup, a worker blocked in a blocking read never reaches its check; either bound the wait or signal the primitive so it wakes and re-checks.
A flag on a single object shared by several pools cancels all of them; keep one token per operation tree, because Ruby has no built-in hierarchy to derive children from.
Thread-local and fiber-local state can be read by the wrong execution context: pass the token as a parameter (or through the job payload) instead of storing it in a Thread.current key.
Ractors cannot share mutable objects like this at all; the token must travel as part of the message, and the cancellation must be delivered as a message too.

variants.name: Asynchronous exception injection with Thread#raise
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby's native way to stop a thread is to inject an asynchronous exception with Thread#raise, which is what Timeout.timeout does; the exception can be raised at any instruction boundary, so it behaves like forced termination from the perspective of the interrupted code. It is a real and widely used realization - and the one Ruby's own ecosystem warns against, precisely because it can fire inside a mutex, an ensure block or a rescue handler and leave shared state inconsistent. Treat it as the emergency lever for foreign or unmodifiable code that cannot be made cooperative, and keep the code that receives it wrapped so cleanup still runs (ensure blocks execute as the unwind proceeds).
variants.code_sketch:
worker = Thread.new do
  begin
    loop { process(queue.pop) }          # no safe points at all
  rescue CancelledOperationError
    cleanup                              # ensure-based cleanup still runs
  end
end

worker.raise(CancelledOperationError)    # asynchronous: lands anywhere
worker.join                              # do not free shared state before this returns
pitfalls: The exception can land between any two instructions: inside a critical section, a rescue clause or an ensure block, so the interrupted code cannot guarantee invariants - only rescue a dedicated cancellation class and only around code written for it.
A broad rescue (rescue => e or rescue Exception) swallows the injected exception and the thread continues as if nothing happened; rescue narrowly and re-raise cancellation.
Thread#raise returns immediately: the target may still be unwinding, so join before releasing anything it touches, and never use it from a signal handler or at_exit that may itself be interrupted.

Timeout.timeout is the same mechanism with a timer attached: a timeout that fires inside an ensure or a mutex is a classic source of corrupted state, which is exactly why cooperative tokens are preferred.
